The approximately 10,000-square-metre facility is located in a modern industrial park in Bang Na, an established distribution hub within the Greater Bangkok metropolitan area, with connectivity to Laem Chabang Port and major manufacturing centres along Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC). The distribution centre provides storage and distribution services for high-value and time-sensitive products, including consumer electronics, semiconductors and automotive cargo. Our investment in Bang Na gives customers additional capacity in this important market while connecting them with DP World’s wider freight and logistics capabilities. By bringing these services together, we help customers reduce complexity, respond more quickly to changing demand and keep goods moving reliably within Thailand and across the Asia Pacific region.” The opening of the Bang Na distribution centre is part of DP World’s continued investment in contract logistics capabilities across Asia Pacific, following recent investments in Singapore and Johor, Malaysia.

items.title: Pressure on India-US trades as Colombo becomes a transhipment hot-spot
items.original_title: Pressure on India-US trades as Colombo becomes a transhipment hot-spot
items.summary: Colombo’s increasing popularity as a transhipment hub is heaping cost pressure onto forwarders and shippers on the India-US tradelane, the Sri Lankan gateway’s newfound revenue stream having provoked a worsening tide of congestion. Recognising India is facing its own congestion issues, particularly at Mundra and Nhava Sheva, CH Robinson said Colombo’s status as a transhipment hot-spot was elevating the risks of rolled cargo. “When mainline services omit Colombo to recover schedules, South India cargo can miss planned connections even when space is available on the onward vessel. Feeder timing, container availability, dwell time during transhipping, and whether the mainline vessel makes its planned Colombo port call determine whether the container can use space,” it said. Consequently, the forwarder warned, the issue cargo owners were being left to grapple with was not just whether they could secure allocations, but whether the feeder and mainline connections on these routings would hold together. Much of the congestion Colombo is contending with is a consequence of vessels and services routing away from their traditional transhipment hubs in the Middle East, amid the war between the US and Iran – a situation that seems to have affected US consumers most.

MOL Ocean Bulk, the group’s Singapore-based capesize bulker operator, signed the agreement with Vale International for vessels scheduled to enter service in 2030. The ships will primarily transport Brazilian iron ore to China and other global destinations. MOL said ethanol could reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by up to 90% against heavy fuel oil, depending on the fuel’s production pathway. The deal forms part of Vale’s shipping decarbonisation strategy and is intended to lower the miner’s Scope 3 emissions from seaborne transport. It also adds to a wider wave of Vale-backed tri-fuel ore carrier commitments, including eight similar 210,000-dwt ships chartered from HMM under 25-year agreements beginning in 2030. items.title: New successful pilot at the Valenciaport Sandbox: a new material “cools” containers without consuming energy
items.original_title: New successful pilot at the Valenciaport Sandbox: a new material “cools” containers without consuming energy
items.summary: The Valenciaport Sandbox adds a new pilot to its track record as a testing ground for innovation in the port and logistics environment. This time, the spotlight was on a new passive radiative cooling film developed by the startup Cooling Photonics, which was tested with very positive results at the Transbase Soler depot last summer, and whose results are now being presented. The trial was made possible thanks to the collaboration of the port community, the Fundación Valenciaport and the support of Opentop, Valenciaport’s open innovation hub, which acted as facilitator, connecting the innovative company with the real-world environment in which its technology could prove its value. A test in real summer conditions This summer, over fifteen consecutive days, four identical 20-foot containers with the same solar exposure were monitored: one untreated as a reference, one with a conventional internal thermal blanket, a third with the material on the roof only, and the fourth with the material on the roof and side walls. A material like this opens up applications of great interest for ports, terminals, logistics operators and depots: Juan Manuel Díez, Head of Innovation at the Port Authority of Valencia, stated that the Valenciaport Sandbox was created so that innovative ideas can prove their value in a real port operations environment, with data gathered on the ground.

items.title: Soybeans Near 5-Week Low
items.original_title: Soybeans Near 5-Week Low
items.summary: Soybean futures fell to around $12.7 per bushel, nearing a five-week low as harvest pressure from an expected record-large US crop weighed on prices. A wet late summer and early autumn slowed the harvest pace, but the arrival of new supplies continued to pressure the market. The harvest was 17% complete as of September 27, matching the five-year average, with the crop rated 58% good or excellent. Expectations of a weaker August soybean crush added pressure, with processors crushing 209.6 million bushels, below the average trade estimate. Weak Chinese demand also weighed on prices as soybeans were excluded from China’s latest US agricultural tariff cuts and remain subject to an additional 10% tariff. Chinese crushers have covered much of their needs through early 2027 with South American supplies, while high inventories and weak margins limit fresh purchases. Still, US export demand remains firm, with weekly sales at 1.03 million tonnes for 2026/27, including 589,400 tonnes to China. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.original_title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.summary: Türkiye’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, while avoiding nearly half a billion euros in health and environmental damage costs and supporting around 1,100 jobs a year, according to a new IMO study. Commissioned by IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 programme in partnership with Türkiye’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure, the study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries carrying vehicles and passengers across 26 ports. The network transports around 25 million passengers and seven million vehicles each year. Significant potential to cut emissions The study found that battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible options across all Ro-Pax and Ro-Ro ferry operations assessed in the Sea of Marmara. It identified an optimum scenario combining hybrid and fully electric vessels to balance emissions reductions and costs. Under this scenario, annual GHG emissions could fall by around 63% by 2050 compared with business-as-usual operations using diesel fuel. The transition would also reduce local air pollution and could avoid an estimated €492 million in cumulative health and environmental damage costs. Going further, converting the entire fleet to fully electric operations could cut GHG emissions by 84% by 2050.

The pipeline restarted on September 22 and tanker loading resumed several days later, with crude exports from Yanbu estimated at about 2m barrels per day. items.original_title: South Africa advances landmark ports shake-up
items.summary: South Africa is pressing ahead with one of the most significant restructurings of its troubled ports sector in decades, with cabinet backing the separation of Transnet National Ports Authority (TNPA) from Transnet and its establishment as a standalone state-owned company. The move would see the country’s national port landlord owned directly by the state rather than sitting within the Transnet group. Cabinet has also approved a feasibility study into bringing in a minority equity partner from one of South Africa’s development finance institutions. South Africa’s ports have endured a prolonged period of congestion, equipment shortages, inadequate maintenance and declining productivity. Durban plunged back into heavy congestion in August, with vessels facing waits of eight to 12 days and some carriers reporting delays of up to 20 days following disruption around the terminal’s operating-system change. Private capital is increasingly central to Pretoria’s attempted ports revival. ICTSI began operating Durban’s flagship Pier 2 terminal this year under a 25-year partnership involving around R11bn ($638m) of investment after a lengthy legal battle delayed the concession. TNPA has also launched private-sector processes covering Cape Town’s multipurpose terminal, a new floating drydock there and the Richards Bay dry bulk terminal, while Transnet last week opened the qualification process for a private partner for the R30bn-R44bn Ngqura manganese corridor.

items.title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.original_title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.summary: Carriers Have Returned to Suez, and the Data Confirms It Maritime media sources state that container shipping is moving from a capacity shortage to a surplus as carriers return to Suez and shorter voyages free up ships. Suez containership transits rose 59% from March to September, from 139 to 221. The growth came from large ships, 300m and above, up to 24,000 TEU, the post-Panamax to ultra-large vessels used on main Asia-Europe services, which rose from 22 to 127 transits a month. Around 100 more large containerships now transit the Suez Canal instead of around Africa, compared to March, cutting one to two weeks off each round trip. Suez routing for Asia-Europe services has recovered to only about a quarter of pre-crisis levels, per Sea-Intelligence. Even a partial return matters, because carriers expanded Asia-Europe capacity by approximately 41% between May 2023 and May 2025 to cover the longer route around Africa, according to Alphaliner, meaning that every service that switches back to Suez frees ships the route no longer needs. Shorter voyages mean each liner service needs fewer ships to keep its schedule, freeing capacity just as Europe-bound demand softens after the summer and ahead of China’s Golden Week holiday (1-7 Oct), when factory closures halt much of China’s export production.

items.summary: Like climbers entering the death zone above 8,000 metres en route to the summit of Everest, VLCCs have entered their own peak: the moment where prices for secondhand tonnage surpass newbuild prices, and sell signs flash hard. These moments tend to be fleeting and have historically been associated with the hottest stages of shipping cycles. The question is how often the market has reached this altitude before, and how long it can survive there. The previous maximum premium for a five-year-old VLCC over a newbuild was 21% in December 2007. Veson data shows a 15-year-old VLCC overtook the newbuild value for the first time on September 27. Danish Ship Finance takes a broader approach, using a monthly secondhand-to-newbuilding price ratio for tankers stretching back to January 2000. Its series identifies 11 distinct episodes, including the current one. “To stay with your analogy: the death zone usually punishes those who linger — but in 2003–08, the market camped up there for nearly six years,” Danish Ship Finance told Splash. The completed episodes have averaged around 12 months, although that number is heavily distorted by the extraordinary 2003-08 supercycle, which accounts for more than half of all the months its tanker index has spent above parity.

items.title: Turkey and UN Broker New Talks on Russia-Ukraine Black Sea Truce
items.original_title: Turkey and UN Broker New Talks on Russia-Ukraine Black Sea Truce
items.summary: Vessels are seen as they await inspection under the Black Sea Grain Initiative, brokered by the United Nations and Turkey, in the southern anchorage of the Bosphorus in Istanbul, Turkey December 11, 2022. REUTERS/Yoruk Isik/File Photo (Bloomberg) — Turkey and the United Nations have set up fresh talks in Russia and Ukraine to discuss a Black Sea ceasefire , trying to coalesce scattered efforts to protect grain shipments as global food prices surge. The meetings will take place in early October, according to a senior diplomat. The initiative, which launched in September with buy-in from other global powers, attempts to replicate a successful 2022 push to secure Black Sea grain shipping. The talks are picking up steam as Russia and Ukraine, which make up more than a quarter of the world’s wheat shipments, increase attacks on each other’s Black Sea port facilities, helping push wheat futures to a three-year high in August. Turkey and the UN bring credibility to the campaign, having also steered the 2022 ceasefire, which ensured the safe passage of grain, fertilizer and food from Ukrainian ports. Russia has set out tough conditions for resurrecting any Black Sea deal, including some sanctions relief and significant military concessions from Ukraine.

items.summary: DP World has welcomed four of Europe’s largest quay cranes to its UK ports, as part of its continued investment to expand capacity and support the growth of UK trade. The first pair of cranes, weighing more than 2,000 tonnes each and standing nearly 150 metres high, taller than world-famous London landmarks such as the London Eye and St Paul’s Cathedral, arrived fully assembled by sea at London Gateway on Friday 25 September, having completed their round the world journey from Shanghai. They will be installed at the new all-electric Berth 5, currently under construction as part of DP World’s £1 billion expansion of the port, which is due to become operational in 2027. The second pair are due to arrive at Southampton next week and follow the delivery of two new cranes in June, bringing the total number servicing the terminal to 16. Capable of consecutive ‘tandem lifts’ of two 40ft containers at once, the new cranes can service the largest container ships currently in operation, including 24,000 TEU megaships, enabling both terminals to accommodate growing trade volumes and the increasing size of vessels serving global shipping routes. • 46% share of UK containerised trade now handled by the combined DP World operations at London Gateway and Southampton.

items.title: Alternative-Fuel Ship Orders Surge to Two-Year High
items.original_title: Alternative-Fuel Ship Orders Surge to Two-Year High
items.summary: CMA CGM's LNG-powered CMA CGM Jacques Saadé under construction at China State Shipbuilding Corporation in 2020. Photo courtesy CMA CGM Alternative-fuel ship orders rebounded sharply in the third quarter, with September delivering the strongest monthly total in nearly two years as LNG remained the dominant choice for new vessels. Shipowners placed orders for 69 alternative-fuelled vessels in September, the highest monthly total since October 2024, according to new figures from DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform. The September activity brought third-quarter orders to 168 vessels, making it the busiest quarter since the third quarter of 2024. “September capped the strongest quarter for alternative-fuelled vessel contracting in the past two years, bringing year-to-date orders comfortably above the level seen at the same point last year.” LNG accounted for 48 of September’s 69 orders, covering containerships, car carriers, bulk carriers and ro-ro cargo vessels. Another 12 orders were for ethanol-fuelled bulk carriers, while nine LPG-fuelled vessels were ordered during the month. DNV warned in its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050 that regulatory outcomes could significantly change the economics of alternative fuels over the operating lives of vessels ordered today. Alternative-fuel-capable tonnage has already grown from just 0.4% of the global fleet in 2020 to 5.2% in 2026, according to DNV, led primarily by LNG and methanol systems.

Newly delivered sistership Ratima Naree went straight to Trafigura Maritime Logistics last month for 12 to 14 months at 107.5% of the BSI 63K, equivalent to around $22,800 per day when the charter started. A couple of weeks later, the 2016-built ultramax Sunisa Naree was fixed to Singapore’s PACC Line for 11 to 13 months at 103% of the same index, then equivalent to about $23,000 per day. The fixture comes as Precious continues to expand its ultramax exposure.

items.original_title: Ships Face Fuel Delays at China’s Zhoushan on Supply Squeeze
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: An aerial view shows a crude oil tanker at an oil terminal off Waidiao island in Zhoushan, Zhejiang province, China January 4, 2023. China Daily via REUTERS Ships are being forced to wait significantly longer to refuel at China’s top bunkering hub of Zhoushan, where the fallout from the US-Iran war has tightened supplies and pushed up prices. Some vessels seeking to refuel at the port south of Shanghai are facing wait times of around one to two weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. Spot prices for very low-sulfur bunker fuel sold at Zhoushan on Tuesday were near their highest level since March, in the early days of the Iran war, according to bunker data provider ClearLynx LLC. That’s more than 25% what the fuel is selling for in Singapore, a competing bunkering hub in Asia. China’s state-owned refiners produced 1.12 million tons of low-sulfur fuel oil in August, a 13% decline from July, according to data from energy information provider JLC. Beijing has long sought to build Zhoushan into a regional bunkering hub to rival Singapore, though the city-state still remains the clear leader for ship refueling. China introduced a fuel oil tax rebate to offer competitive prices to attract Asia-bound commercial fleets while encouraging domestic refiners to boost low-sulfur fuel oil output.

items.title: Supreme court clears way for Świnoujście deepwater container terminal
items.original_title: Supreme court clears way for Świnoujście deepwater container terminal
items.summary:
Poland's Supreme Administrative Court in Warsaw has dismissed a cassation appeal brought by the German environmental association Lebensraum Vorpommern against the planned deepwater container terminal in Świnoujście, the Szczecin and Świnoujście Seaports Authority announced. The appeal had challenged the project's environmental approvals through the Polish administrative courts, and its dismissal ends that line of litigation, removing one of the main legal obstacles to construction.

The terminal, now branded Cape Pomerania (Przylądek Pomorski), is designed to let the port handle the largest ocean-going container vessels and lift Poland's container capacity on the western coast. The court decision completes the environmental and administrative review process in the Polish judiciary. The announcement did not add new details on specifications, timetable or investment value beyond what the port authority has published before.
items.why: Removes a legal risk to the largest investment in the Szczecin–Świnoujście complex; expect the construction timetable, hinterland traffic and competitive landscape around Świnoujście to firm up.

items.title: EU proposes overhaul of maritime ETS, MRV and FuelEU, extending carbon costs to smaller cargo ships
items.original_title: EU proposes overhaul of maritime ETS, MRV and FuelEU, extending carbon costs to smaller cargo ships
items.summary:
The European Commission's July 2026 proposals would reshape the rules for maritime emissions, targeting a 90% cut in shipping greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. A new instrument, SMAP (Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion), would channel about EUR 15bn between 2028 and 2040 into clean fuels and propulsion.

From 2031 the EU ETS would extend to general cargo and offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnes, partly aligning with the UK ETS. The definition of offshore ship would move to an activity-based test, potentially capturing more vessels serving offshore wind farms. The separate ETS, MRV and FuelEU Maritime reporting systems would be merged into one compliance framework.

The package still needs agreement from the Council and Parliament, with political agreement targeted for Q1 2027 and implementation by 2029, and must be coordinated with the IMO Net Zero Framework.
